Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:1:
Gate One – On the Explanation of Teshuvah and Its Foundations.
Among the good things that the Blessed Name has done for His creatures is that He prepared for them a way to rise up out of the pit of their deeds and flee the snare of their transgressions, to spare their soul from the grave and turn back His wrath from them, and He taught them and warned them to return to Him when they sin against Him, out of the abundance of His goodness and uprightness, for He knows their inclination, as it is said (Psalms 25:8), "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore He guides sinners in the way." And even if they multiplied transgression and rebellion, and dealt treacherously as treacherous men deal, He did not close the gates of repentance before them, as it is said (Isaiah 31:6), "Return to Him from whom you have deeply revolted," and it is said (Jeremiah 3:22), "Return, backsliding children, I will heal your backslidings." And we have been warned about teshuvah in several places in the Torah, and it has been made clear that teshuvah is accepted even when the sinner returns only because of his many troubles — how much more so if he returns out of fear of the Lord and love of Him — as it is said (Deuteronomy 4:30), "When you are in distress and all these things have come upon you, in the end of days, you will return to the Lord your God and heed His voice." And it has been made clear in the Torah that the Lord helps those who return when their own natural strength cannot reach it, and He renews within them a pure spirit to attain the level of love of Him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 30:2), "And you shall return to the Lord your God and heed His voice, according to all that I command you this day, you and your children, with all your heart and all your soul." And it says at the end of the matter (Deuteronomy 30:6), "And the Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring" — to attain love of Him. And the Prophets and the Writings spoke always of the matter of teshuvah, until all the foundations of teshuvah came to be spelled out in their words, as will be explained.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:2: And know, that when the sinner delays returning from his sin, his punishment grows heavier upon him every day, for he knows that wrath has gone out against him and that he has a refuge to flee to, and that refuge is teshuvah — yet he stands still in his rebellion and remains in his wickedness, though it is in his power to come out of the overthrow, and he does not dread the anger and the fury; therefore his wickedness is great. And our Sages of blessed memory said of this matter (Kohelet Rabbah 7:32): a parable of a band of bandits whom the king confined in prison; they dug a tunnel, broke through, and escaped, and one of them remained. The warden of the prison came and saw the tunnel dug through and that man still held captive, and he struck him with his staff, saying to him: Fool! Is not the tunnel dug through before you — why did you not hasten to save your life?
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:3: And such delay of teshuvah is found only among the ignorant masses, who lie asleep and do not take it to heart, having neither knowledge nor understanding to hasten to save their souls; and some of them are cast off from the Blessed Name and do not believe in the punishment of sin. And our Sages of blessed memory said (Berachot 19a): If you saw a Torah scholar commit a transgression at night, do not suspect him of it by day, for he has certainly already done teshuvah.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:4: And further, consider the great evil of one who delays his teshuvah. For had he not delayed, he would by now have already returned, sighing in bitterness of heart, trembling and anxious, his eye streaming with grief, so that were his inclination to confront him a second time and the sin come within his reach, he would subdue his inclination, remembering the cup of bitterness that had already passed over him, and would not drink of it again — as it is said (Psalms 4:5), "Tremble and sin not," which means: tremble and grieve over what you have sinned, and sin no more; for above it mentions their sin, saying (Psalms 4:3), "You seek falsehood, selah." And proof of this interpretation is that it says "tremble," in the sense of (Genesis 45:24), "Do not become agitated on the way," and (Habakkuk 3:16), "and beneath me I tremble" — their meaning is grief over what has passed and over the present, and it does not say "fear" or "be afraid." But when the sinner delays his return, then when the sin again comes within his reach he falls into his snare just as he fell the first time, and his final iniquity grows very great, and his wickedness rises up before the Lord — for at the outset he had not considered that the ruling inclination would suddenly come upon him again; but after he saw the weakness of his own strength, and that the hand of his inclination had overpowered him, and that it was mightier than he — he ought to have recognized that he was exposed, and to have taken counsel with himself to add to himself the fear of the Lord, and to cast dread of Him upon his soul, and to save it from the ambush of his inclination, and to guard himself from his iniquity. And Solomon, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 26:11), "As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly" — its meaning is that a dog eats repugnant things, and when it vomits them, they become still more repugnant, yet it returns to eat them again; so is the way of the fool — he does a shameful deed, and when he repeats it, it becomes still more shameful, as we have explained.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:5: The second point: one who repeats his sin finds teshuvah difficult, because the sin has become to him as though permitted, and by this his sin grows very heavy, as it is said (Jeremiah 3:5), "Will He bear a grudge forever, will He keep it to the end? Behold, you have spoken, and have done evil things, and have prevailed (vatuchal)." The meaning of "vatuchal" is that the evil deeds have become to you as a permitted thing, within your power and license — in the sense of (Deuteronomy 12:17), "You may not (lo tuchal) eat within your gates," which the Targum renders "you have no permission." And our Sages of blessed memory said (Yoma 86b): "Once a person transgresses a sin and repeats it, it becomes to him as though permitted." And our Sages of blessed memory said of one who transgressed a sin and repeated it, that from then on, if he intends to commit the transgression and is prevented by circumstance and does not commit it, his evil intention is joined together with an actual deed, and of him it is said (Jeremiah 6:19), "Behold, I bring evil upon this people, the fruit of their own thoughts."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:6: Now understand and hear this, for it is a great foundation. True, there are among the righteous those who stumble in sin at times, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 7:20), "For there is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin" — yet they subdue their inclination and turn their faces from it, and if they fall into sin once, they do not repeat it, but feel disgust with themselves and return in teshuvah. But whoever does not guard himself against a sin he knows well, and does not take it upon himself to be careful of it — even if it is among the lighter transgressions, even though he is careful about every other transgression in the Torah — the Sages of Israel called him (Chullin 4b) "an apostate regarding one thing," and he is counted among the wicked, and his sin is too great to bear. For if a servant were to say to his master, "All that you tell me I will do, except for one thing" — he has already thrown off his master's yoke and does whatever seems right in his own eyes. And of this matter it is said (Deuteronomy 27:26), "Cursed be he who does not uphold the words of this Torah, to do them" — its meaning is: whoever does not accept upon himself to fulfill all the words of the Torah from beginning to end. And this is shown by its saying "who does not uphold... to do," and not saying "who does not do them."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:7: And know further, that one who repeats the same transgression ten times, even though he is careful about every other transgression, is considered as one who has transgressed distinct, separate transgressions. And so our Sages of blessed memory said (Makkot 21a): if they say to a nazirite, "Do not drink," and he drinks, "Do not drink," and he drinks again, he is lashed at the end for each and every instance, just as in the law of one who eats forbidden meat, an unclean animal, or forbidden fat and blood.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:8: And indeed we have seen that the sins of this generation have multiplied because of this, for there are many people who do not take upon themselves to be careful about certain known transgressions, and all their lives they are not careful about them, but treat them as though permitted; and even were they to act this way regarding only one transgression, it would already be a grave sickness of the soul, as we have explained — how much more so when they are lax regarding many warnings, and among them some of the gravest: such as a needless oath, cursing one's fellow or oneself by God's Name, mentioning the Name of Heaven in vain or in an impure place or with unclean hands, turning one's eye away from the poor, evil speech (lashon hara), needless hatred, haughtiness of heart, intimidating others, gazing at forbidden sights of immorality, and neglect of Torah study, which outweighs all of them — and many more like these. We have written some of them for the people of this generation, to remind and to warn them. And it is likewise fitting for every penitent to write in a scroll the things in which he stumbled and the commandments he fell short in fulfilling, and to read from his scroll of remembrance every day.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:9: Now, there are many levels of teshuvah, and according to those levels a person draws near to the Holy One, blessed be He. And indeed, for every teshuvah forgiveness is found, but the soul is not purified with a complete purity, so that the sins become as though they had never been, except when a person purifies his heart and prepares his spirit as will be explained. And so it is written (Psalms 32:2), "Fortunate is the man to whom the Lord does not reckon iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit." This is like a garment that requires laundering: a little laundering will remove the foul odor from it, but the more it is laundered, the whiter it becomes. And so it is written (Psalms 51:4), "Wash me thoroughly of my iniquity," and the soul is cleansed of sin in proportion to how one cleanses one's heart, as it is said (Jeremiah 4:14), "Wash your heart of wickedness, O Jerusalem." And our Sages of blessed memory said (Avodah Zarah 19a) on "Fortunate is the man who fears the Lord" (Psalms 112:1) — "while he is still a man" — meaning that the finest teshuvah of a person is in the days of his youth, while his strength is still upon him and he can overpower his inclination. Yet every teshuvah is of avail, as it is said (Psalms 90:3), "You return man to dust, and say, Return, children of man," and our Sages of blessed memory said (Jerusalem Talmud, Chagigah 2:1) — even until the crushing of the soul. Now let us explain the foundations of teshuvah.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:10: The First Foundation – Regret: Let his heart understand that it is evil and bitter that he has forsaken the Lord, and let him take to heart that there is punishment, vengeance, and payment for iniquity, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:35), "Vengeance and payment are Mine," and it is said (Job 19:29), "Be in dread of the sword, for wrath brings the punishments of the sword." And let him regret his evil deeds, and say in his heart: What have I done? How was the dread of God not before my eyes, and I did not tremble at the rebukes concerning iniquity and the evil judgments, for many are the sorrows of the wicked? I did not have compassion on my own body, nor did my own eye spare it from destruction, for the sake of the pleasure of a single moment, and I have become like a man who robs and plunders and eats and is satisfied, knowing that after he has eaten and drunk, the Judge will grind his teeth with gravel, as it is said (Proverbs 20:17), "Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel." And worse than this — I was cruel toward my own precious soul, and it became defiled by the idols of my inclination; and what did all its possessions avail it, if it is evil in the eyes of its Master? And how did I exchange a passing world for a world that stands forever, eternally? How did I become like the beasts, following after my inclination like a horse or a mule without understanding, and stray from the way of reason? Behold, the Creator breathed into my nostrils a living soul, a wise heart and a good understanding, to know Him and to fear before Him, and to rule over the body and all its offshoots, just as He gave it dominion over the other creatures that do not speak, since it is precious and honored in His eyes; and after I was created for this purpose, and the opposite came to be in me — why then do I have life? As it is said (Proverbs 21:16), "A man who strays from the way of reason will rest in the assembly of the departed." And furthermore, I have not even acted as befits a beast, but have fallen lower than it, for an ox knows its owner and a donkey its master's trough, and I did not know and did not consider, and I sent my soul free from its Master, and I tasted its honey but forgot its end, and I robbed and plundered, and trampled upon the poor, and did not remember the day of death, which will leave before my soul nothing but my body and my dust. And this matter which we have explained is what Jeremiah, peace upon him, spoke of (Jeremiah 8:6), "No man repents of his wickedness, saying: What have I done."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:11: The Second Foundation – Abandoning the Sin: that he abandon his evil ways and resolve with all his heart that he will no longer return to that way, and that if he has done iniquity, he will not do so again, as it is said (Ezekiel 33:11), "Return, return from your evil ways," and it is said (Isaiah 55:7), "Let the wicked man abandon his way." And know, that one who sinned by way of chance occurrence — that a desire arose in him and his inclination grew strong and overpowered him, and his thoughts and senses were not able to free themselves when it confronted him, and did not hasten to rebuke the sea of desire so that it would dry up, so that the inclination hunted him in its nets and he fell into its snares in accordance with his moment and his hour, this being because the spirit of the evil inclination terrified him, and not because it was his own wish and will to find his iniquity and to do so again afterward — the beginning of this man's teshuvah is regret, and to place grief in his heart over his sin and to have a soul that is afflicted and bitter as wormwood; after that, he should add the fear of the Lord to his soul every day, and place the dread of God in his heart at all times, until his heart is firm and secure in the Lord — for if he continues, and his inclination passes over him and confronts him time after time, and his desire grows strong upon him as in the first instance, his heart will not be seduced by it, and he will abandon his way, as it is said (Proverbs 28:13), "But he who confesses and forsakes them will find mercy" — it mentions first "confesses," referring to regret and confession, and afterward "forsakes." But the man who continually stands firm on an evil path, and treads upon his sins every day, and repeats his folly and returns to his course many times over, and at all times loves evil, and sets the stumbling-block of his iniquity — meaning desire and inclination — before himself, his will and his purpose, so that nothing he plans to do is withheld from him — the beginning of this man's teshuvah is to abandon his way and his evil intent, and to resolve to fulfill and accept upon himself never to sin again; afterward he should regret his corrupt deeds and confess, in order to return to the Lord, as it is said (Isaiah 55:7), "Let the wicked forsake his way and the man of iniquity his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord and He will have mercy on him." And the parable for this is one who holds an unclean creeping thing and comes to immerse and be purified — he must first put down the creeping thing, and only then immerse and become pure; for as long as the creeping thing is in his hand, his impurity remains upon him and the immersion is of no avail. So too, abandoning the thought of sin is the casting away of the creeping thing, and regret over having sinned, confession, and prayer take the place of the immersion. And when suffering and pain come upon the wicked man whose constant purpose is to walk in his guilt, he should first be chastened and turn back from the evil thought he had conceived, and cut off his deeds from his own hands. And the parable for this is a calf that is struck with the ox-goad to direct its furrows; so too, one who stands firm on a bad path should first accept discipline, to abandon the ways of death and walk the straight way, as it is said (Jeremiah 31:18), "I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself: You have chastised me, and I was chastised, like a calf unaccustomed to the yoke." And it says further afterward (Jeremiah 31:19), "For after I turned back, I regretted" — meaning: after You chastised me and I was chastised and I turned back from my evil way, I regretted afterward and repented over what had passed of the words of my iniquities. And thus the whole matter we have explained becomes clear to you from this.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:12: The Third Foundation – Grief: let him search his innermost being and consider how very great is the wickedness of one who has rebelled against his Maker. And let him magnify grief in his heart, and let a storm rage within his thoughts, and let him sigh in bitterness of heart. For it may be that he will regret and feel bad about the sin he committed, yet not fulfill his obligation in this regard — for even the loss of a single coin is grievous in a person's eyes, but if he lost his entire wealth through some terrible matter and came out stripped of all his possessions, his soul would mourn over it, his sighing would grow heavy, and his soul would be bitter to him; and so too over great and many troubles his pain is perpetual, and grief fills his heart by day. And how much more fitting is it that one who rebelled against the Blessed Name, and corrupted and made abominable his deeds before Him, and did not remember his Maker who created him from nothing and dealt kindly with him, and whose hand guides him at all times, and who preserves his soul every single moment — should feel pain and sigh, and how could his heart have been so full as to provoke Him, and how could the sinner's eyes have been so plastered over as not to perceive with understanding heart? And the intelligent man whose eyes have been opened will engrave these things upon his heart, and they will come into the innermost chambers of his spirit.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:13: And the levels and degrees of teshuvah correspond to the greatness of the bitterness and the intensity of the grief. And this is the teshuvah that comes by way of purity of soul and clarity of its intellect, for according to a person's intellect, and to the degree that his eyes are opened, his griefs and thoughts over the abundance of his wretchedness will grow and become exceedingly powerful — as it is said (Isaiah 57:16), "For I will not contend forever, nor will I be wrathful to the end, for the spirit would grow faint before Me, and the souls which I have made." Its meaning is: when the spirit that is from before Me — for it is of the higher realms — grows faint and suffers, and the souls that I have made grow faint, I will not contend further nor be wrathful, for how could I not show favor and mercy upon a precious soul that is from before Me, and souls which I have made? Therefore the iniquity becomes lighter in proportion as the anguish and the sighing over it grow heavier, for the grief comes from the purity of the higher soul, and this finds more favor than would be found through an abundance of bodily afflictions and pains. And the parable for this is that a king has compassion on his own attendants, raised in his own household and close to him, who are among the honored nobility of the land, and grants them pardon more readily than his compassion upon those who are distant and lowly; and it says "souls which I have made," because of their nearness to the higher realms, even though the body too, and everything, are the work of His hands — and likewise (Exodus 32:16), "and the tablets were the work of God." And our Sages of blessed memory further said (Niddah 31a) that there are three partners in the forming of a person — his father, his mother, and the Holy One, blessed be He — and since the father and mother have no share in the soul, therefore it says, "souls which I have made." And its saying "souls which I have made" points back to its saying, "for the spirit is from before Me," for its meaning is as we have explained.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:14: And David the king, peace upon him, said (Psalms 38:10), "O Lord, all my desire is before You, and my sighing is not hidden from You." Its meaning is: all my desire is revealed before You, for it is for nothing but Your service; and You know my sighing, for it is not over worldly affairs and things that perish, but only over my sin and the shortness of my reach in Your service. And one of those who cast themselves before Him in the fullness of their worth said: My sighing over the dread of You has driven sighs away from me; my worry over the shortness of my reach in Your service has driven worries away from me.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:15: The Fourth Foundation – Suffering in Practice: as it is said (Joel 2:12), "Yet even now, says the Lord, return to Me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with lamentation." And our Sages of blessed memory said, the heart and the eyes are the two brokers of sin, and so it is written (Numbers 15:39), "And you shall not go astray after your heart and after your eyes." Therefore by this the iniquity of these two brokers is atoned: in the measure of their teshuvah, corresponding to the measure of their backsliding, so that the iniquity of the sinners' hearts is atoned through their bitterness and sighing — through the breaking they inflict upon themselves — as it is written (Isaiah 57:16), "For the spirit would grow faint before Me," and it is said (Psalms 51:19), "A broken and crushed heart, O God, You will not despise." And the parable for this is drawn from unclean vessels that, once broken, are purified from their impurity, as it is written (Leviticus 11:35), "An oven or stove shall be broken down." And the iniquity of the eyes is atoned through tears, as it is said (Psalms 119:136), "Streams of water flow down from my eyes, because they [others] have not kept Your Torah." It does not say, "because I did not keep Your Torah," but says "they have not kept it," for it was they, the eyes, who brought about the sin — therefore I have brought down streams of water.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:16: The Fifth Foundation – Worry: that he worry and be afraid of the punishment for his iniquities. For there are iniquities for which teshuvah suspends the atonement and sufferings scour it away, as it is written (Psalms 38:19), "For I will declare my iniquity, I am in dread of my sin." The matter of grief concerns what has already passed, and the matter of worry concerns what is yet to come. And there is a further reason he should worry: perhaps he is falling short of the full obligation of teshuvah in his suffering and bitterness and fasting and weeping; and even if he has multiplied his suffering and multiplied his weeping, he should still tremble and fear that perhaps, in proportion to this, he has multiplied guilt, and has not fully discharged all his obligation of affliction and of weeping his soul out in fasting. And one who has contemplated the greatness of the Creator's service demanded of His creatures, and that there is no limit to the evil of one who defies His word, will find that however much he adds to his service and to the ways of teshuvah, it is surely a small thing, and it will appear little in his own eyes. And Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 14:16), "A wise man fears and turns from evil" — its meaning is that the wise man, though he turns from evil with all his might, still fears and trembles, lest perhaps he has not fully discharged his obligation, and has not been careful as the law requires. And likewise (Proverbs 28:6), "than one perverse in his ways though he be rich" — even though he is rich. And so our Sages of blessed memory said in the Yelamdenu: Do not interpret "a wise man fears and turns from evil," but rather "a wise man turns from evil and fears" — and the end of the verse proves this (ibid.), "but a fool becomes enraged and is confident" — it speaks of the traits of the fool, which are the opposite of the trait of the wise man, for the fool becomes enraged, and nevertheless is confident that no iniquity or harm will befall him. And the man of anger is prone to transgressions and given over to harm, as it is said (Proverbs 29:22), "and a man of wrath abounds in transgression," and it is said (Proverbs 25:28), "Like a city broken down without a wall is a man who has no restraint over his spirit."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:17: And further, the penitent should worry lest his inclination overpower him, as our Sages of blessed memory said, "Do not trust in yourself until the day of your death" — how much more so a man whose heart has already once been defeated by it; for it is fitting to guard oneself always from the inclination, which lies in ambush at every moment, and to add the fear of the Lord to his soul day by day, and this will be for him a stronghold when all the breakers of the inclination that renew themselves in the future pass over him.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:18: And Solomon the king, peace upon him, spoke of the matter of teshuvah and set out this matter in detail, opening his words by saying (Proverbs 28:12), "When the righteous exult there is great glory, but when the wicked arise, men hide themselves." Its meaning is: the righteous glorify and honor people for every good quality found in them, while the wicked search out the blemishes of people and their errors, in order to lower them — even though those very people may already have abandoned those deeds and returned in teshuvah. Afterward it says (Proverbs 28:13), "He who conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will find mercy." For even though the penitent need not reveal his sins to other people — as may be understood from what it said, "when the wicked arise, men hide themselves" — nevertheless he is obligated to confess them, as it is said (Psalms 32:5), "I made known my sin to You and did not conceal my iniquity," and it is said (Jeremiah 2:35), "Behold, I will bring you to judgment, because you say, I have not sinned." And the Sages of Israel, of blessed memory, explained that sometimes "he who conceals his transgressions will not prosper" applies to transgressions between man and his fellow, for he has no atonement until he returns what he robbed, or the stolen or extorted property, and until he seeks forgiveness from the one he distressed, or whose face he shamed, or about whom he spoke evil speech; or to transgressions between man and God that have become publicly known, for one who commits transgressions in public desecrates the Name (and Rashi, of blessed memory, in the chapter on Yom Kippur, explains it differently — see there) — and he is obligated to lament and to mourn over them before other people, in order to sanctify the Name. And this is what is written (Jeremiah 31:18), "For after I turned back, I regretted, and after I came to know myself, I struck upon my thigh" — the meaning of "I regretted" is regret and grief, for the essence of teshuvah is in the bitterness of the heart, as we have explained; and "after I came to know myself, I struck upon my thigh" means: after I became known to other people and my sins were made public, I mourned through actions visible to other people, as in (Ezekiel 21:17), "striking upon the thigh," and it is said (Job 33:27), "He looks upon men and says, I have sinned and perverted what was right."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:19: "But he who confesses and forsakes them will find mercy" — its meaning is: even though the foundations of teshuvah are three — regret, confession, and abandonment of the sin — regret and confession are included in "confesses," for one who confesses regrets, and there is no teshuvah less than these three; for one who regrets and confesses but does not abandon the sin is like one who immerses while still holding the unclean creature in his hand. But "he who confesses and forsakes will find mercy," for he is truly a penitent, even though teshuvah has many further levels, as we have explained.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:20: It says further afterward (Proverbs 28:14), "Fortunate is the man who fears always, but he who hardens his heart will fall into evil." Its meaning is: even though he has confessed and abandoned the sin, he must still fear always, lest he has not fully discharged the obligation of teshuvah, for it requires many levels, and he should add strength every day to attain those levels; he should also fear lest his inclination be renewed against him, and he should guard against it always, and add the fear of the Lord to his soul continually, and pray always to the Lord to help him toward teshuvah and to save him from his inclination. And "he who hardens his heart will fall into evil" refers to one who says in his heart, "I have fully discharged my obligation of teshuvah," and does not strive continually to attain the levels of teshuvah and to add fear to his soul — he will be punished for this, for he is haughty of heart and does not recognize the deficiency of his own soul; and if he does not recognize the greatness of his obligation to make his ways ever more excellent before the Lord, he also fails to guard himself from his inclination, which lies in ambush for him always — therefore he will fall into the hand of his inclination.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:21: The Sixth Foundation – Shame: as it is said (Jeremiah 31:18), "I was ashamed, and even confounded, for I bore the reproach of my youth." Now, the sinner is greatly ashamed to commit transgressions before other people, and he is humiliated should they perceive and recognize his transgressions — how then can he not be ashamed before the Blessed Creator? And this is only because the Blessed Name is distant from his innermost thoughts; therefore he is ashamed before creatures, but not ashamed before the Blessed Creator. And our Sages of blessed memory said that at the time of the passing of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, his disciples said to him, "Our teacher, bless us." He said to them: "May it be His will that the fear of Heaven be upon you as is the fear of flesh and blood." They said to him: "Our teacher, no more than that?" He said to them: "Would that it be so! Know that when a person commits a transgression in secret, he says, would that no man see me."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:22: And the highest level in this is for a person to be humiliated over his iniquities before the Blessed Name. And the matter of humiliation is the very feeling of shame together with the changing of the color of one's face, as it is said (Psalms 69:8), "Shame has covered my face." And everywhere you will find "humiliation" mentioned after "shame," for it exceeds mere shame — (Ezekiel 36:32), "be ashamed and humiliated," (Jeremiah 31:18), "I was ashamed, and even humiliated." And when the sinner sees that the Blessed Name overlooks his iniquity and is patient with him, and does not exact retribution from him, and has not dealt with him according to his sins nor requited him according to his iniquities, he should add shame to his heart. Behold, one who sins against a king of flesh and blood and betrays him, and the king nevertheless forgives him, is ashamed before him; and so it is written (Ezekiel 16:63), "so that you may remember and be ashamed, and never open your mouth again because of your humiliation, when I have forgiven you for all that you have done." And our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever commits a deed and is ashamed of it, all his iniquities are forgiven him. And so we find regarding Saul, who said (I Samuel 28:15), "He no longer answers me, neither by prophets nor by dreams," and he did not mention the Urim and Tummim, for he was ashamed to mention them, because he had slain Nob, the city of the priests; and Samuel said to him (I Samuel 28:19), "Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me" — meaning, with me, in my own compartment [of the World to Come]. And a person attains the level of shame by secluding himself to contemplate the greatness of the Name, and how very great is the wickedness of one who defies His word, and by remembering always that the Name sees his deeds, examines his innermost being, and observes his thoughts.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:23: The Seventh Foundation – Submission with a Whole Heart, and Lowliness: for one who knows his Creator will know how bowed down and lowly is one who transgresses His word, and how diminished is his worth, as it is said (Psalms 15:4), "in whose eyes a vile person is despised," and it is said (Job 15:16), "how much more one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks iniquity like water"; (Jeremiah 6:30), "Refuse silver they are called of him." Therefore let him be submissive and lowly in his own eyes. And David the king, peace upon him, when confessing his sin upon Nathan the prophet's coming to him, said at the end of his words (Psalms 51:19), "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and crushed heart, O God, You will not despise." "A broken spirit" means a lowly spirit. From this we learn that submission is among the foundations of teshuvah, for this psalm is the foundation established for the foundations of teshuvah. And through submission a person finds favor with the Lord, as it is said (Isaiah 66:2), "to the poor and of a contrite spirit," and it is said concerning teshuvah (Isaiah 57:14-15), "And He said: Cast up, cast up, clear the way... For thus said the High and Exalted One who inhabits eternity, and Holy is His Name: I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with the crushed and lowly of spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly and to revive the heart of the contrite." We learn from this that submission is among the foundations of teshuvah. And likewise the rest of that whole passage speaks of the penitent (Isaiah 57:16-18), "For I will not contend forever...", "for the iniquity of his covetousness I was angered...", "I have seen his ways and I will heal him and lead him..." Its meaning is: I have seen his ways in submission, as it says, "and with the crushed and lowly of spirit," and in bitterness of heart, as it says, "for the spirit would grow faint before Me"; and "I will heal him" — for I will forgive his iniquity, as in (Hosea 14:5), "I will heal their backsliding," (Isaiah 6:10), "and turn back and be healed"; and "I will lead him" — I will help him toward abandoning the sin and strengthen him against his inclination.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:24: And know that the levels of submission are many, as will be explained, God willing, in the Gates of Humility. And the highest level of the submission required by the path of teshuvah is that he magnify and glorify the service of the Lord, and not credit himself with the good, for everything becomes small in his eyes compared to what he is obligated to do in the service of the Lord; therefore he should submit and serve in a hidden, modest manner, and not covet honor for his honorable deeds, nor seek human glory for his glorious acts, but conceal them from people's knowledge as far as possible.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:25: And this matter is set forth as a foundation of teshuvah, explained in the words of the prophet, peace upon him, as it is said (Micah 6:6), "With what shall I approach the Lord, shall I bow myself before God on high?" Its meaning: with what shall I approach the Lord for the abundance of His kindnesses — for he had mentioned earlier in the passage the kindnesses of the Blessed Name — and with what shall I bow myself before God on high, for the abundance of my sins? And it mentions "God on high" to teach and to make known how fitting it is that one who has defied Him who is exalted above all should bow down and submit. And it explains the matter further: "Shall I approach Him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will the Lord be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I offer them to approach Him for the abundance of His kindnesses? Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression" — to show my submission and my bowing down for the abundance of my sin, for I recognize the immensity of my transgression, so that it would be fitting to give my firstborn as an offering for my transgression, for it is very great and mighty — "the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul"? It mentions "my firstborn" regarding the transgression (pesha) and "the fruit of my body" regarding the sin (chatat), for pesha is rebellion, as our Sages of blessed memory said, and it is greater than chatat. And what teshuvah truly is: "He has told you, man, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you: only to do justice and to love kindness" — for this is chosen above burnt offerings and meal-offerings to approach the Lord for His kindnesses — "and to walk humbly with your God" — this is the essence of your submission and bowing down, to serve the Lord in walking humbly, for this shows your submission, that you do not covet honor for your honorable deeds, even for those qualities in which the Creator does not desire His creatures to take pride, such as wealth and strength and various forms of worldly wisdom, but only in understanding and knowing the Blessed Name, as it is said (Jeremiah 9:22), "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom..."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:26: And further, the penitent is obligated in submission because he is obligated to remove from his soul the traits that cause sin and bring about transgressions.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:27: And pride brings about many transgressions, and strengthens a person's evil inclination against him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 8:14), "And your heart grows haughty, and you forget the Lord your God," and it is said (Proverbs 21:4), "Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the tillage of the wicked, is sin." Its meaning is that pride is the tillage-ground of the wicked, for from it sins grow fruitful, as it is said, "and your heart grows haughty, and you forget"; and it is said (Psalms 10:2), "In the pride of the wicked the poor is hotly pursued," and it is said (Psalms 31:19), "who speak arrogantly against the righteous with pride," and it is said (Ezekiel 32:24), "who spread their terror in the land of the living." And just as people till the ground in a field in order to make the seed fruitful and gather abundant crops, so the wicked make pride the tillage-ground of their hearts and sow in it evil thoughts, to give birth to and cause to grow the transgressions that are the fruit of their thoughts — figuratively, as the prophet said, "and it sprouted like hemlock, justice..." And what it says, "sin" (chatat), means: the tillage-ground of the wicked is a tillage-ground of sin, encompassing many sins, as in (Jeremiah 17:1), "the sin of Judah" — or its meaning may be "and sin," as in (Habakkuk 3:11), "sun, moon." And the point is that, aside from pride causing sins, the trait itself is a sin, as it is said (Proverbs 16:5), "An abomination to the Lord is every proud heart." And a proud man is handed over into his own inclination's power, for the help of the Lord is not with him, since he is an abomination to the Lord.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:28: And further, the penitent is obligated to submit himself and to accept to conduct himself in the manner our Sages of blessed memory taught: "Be exceedingly lowly of spirit before every person." And he should learn from this not to become angry and not to be exacting with his fellows; and also, regarding everything he hears, he should not take to heart to react in accordance with his natural inclination toward strict justice — this passing over one's own attributes atones for one's iniquities, as our Sages of blessed memory said: "Whoever passes over his own attributes, they pass over all his transgressions for him" — measure for measure. And this is a most honorable opening for hope, and it is said (Lamentations 3:29-30), "Let him put his mouth in the dust, perhaps there is hope; let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him, let him be filled with reproach."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:29: The Eighth Foundation – Submission in Practice: that he conduct himself with a soft answer, as it is said (Proverbs 15:1), "A soft answer turns away wrath," and with a lowered voice, for this is in the way of lowliness, as it is said (Isaiah 29:4), "And you shall be brought down, you shall speak out of the ground, and your speech shall be low out of the dust" — the opposite of what is said of the proud rich man (Proverbs 18:23), "but the rich answers harshly." And he should not busy himself with fine clothing and ornaments, as it is said (Exodus 33:5), "Now therefore put off your ornaments from yourself," and it is said of Ahab (I Kings 21:27), "and he fasted, and lay in sackcloth, and walked softly (at)," and the Blessed Name said of this, "Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself?" And the matter of "walked softly" is the opposite of the way of kings, who walk with great retinue and the noise of tumult. And his eyes should always be lowered, as it is said (Job 22:29), "and he saves the one of downcast eyes." And these signs of submission — a soft answer, a lowered voice, and downcast eyes — will remind him to keep his heart submissive.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:30: The Ninth Foundation – Breaking Physical Desire: let him take to heart that desire has brought calamity upon his soul, causing it to sin and drawing iniquity along with cords of vanity; and let him make a vow to keep the path of teshuvah, to separate himself from pleasures, and not to be drawn after his desire even in matters that are permitted, and to conduct himself in ways of abstinence, eating only enough to satisfy his soul and sustain his body, as it is said (Proverbs 13:25), "The righteous eats to satisfy his soul." And he should not approach a woman except to fulfill the commandment of procreation, or the marital duty (onah); for as long as a person follows after desire, he is drawn after the offshoots of the material substance, and grows distant from the way of the rational soul, and then his inclination overpowers him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:15), "And Jeshurun grew fat and kicked," and it is said (Deuteronomy 32:8[15]), "lest you eat and be satisfied... and your heart grow haughty," and it is said (Proverbs 30:9), "lest I be full and deny." And our Sages of blessed memory said: there is a small organ in a person — feed it, it hungers; starve it, it is sated.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:31: Now, the desire placed in a person's heart is the root of all his actions; therefore if he sets his desire in order, so that instead of all his limbs serving it, it draws them after the intellect, and they attach themselves to it and serve it, all his deeds will be made proper, as it is said (Proverbs 21:8), "but as for the pure, his work is upright," and it is said (Proverbs 13:19), "Desire fulfilled (nihyah) is sweet to the soul" — "nihyah" is in the sense of "broken," as in (Daniel 8:27), "I was overcome and sick." It says that when a person breaks his desire even in permitted matters, through this the soul will succeed, and this trait will be sweet to it, for the intellect will raise its hand and prevail — "but it is an abomination to fools to turn from evil." The fools are those who do not break their desire, and continually pursue human pleasures, so that when their desire encounters the path of sin and every evil thing, they do not turn away from it; and they are called fools for their pursuit of pleasures, as it is said (Proverbs 21:20), "but a foolish man swallows it up," and it is said (Isaiah 5:11), "Woe to those who rise early in the morning to pursue strong drink... and the harp and the lute... but they do not regard the work of the Lord...", and it is said (Proverbs 13:25), "but the belly of the wicked shall want," and it is said (Malachi 2:3), "and I will spread dung upon your faces, the dung of your festivals," and our Sages of blessed memory said: these are people whose every day is like a festival [of indulgence]. And it is said (Proverbs 18:1), "He who separates himself seeks his own desire, he breaks out against all sound wisdom." Its meaning is: whoever seeks to go after his own desire and will separates himself from every companion and friend, for lover and friend grow distant from him, since people's desires and traits differ — one man's will is not another's; but if he walks in the way of the intellect, then companions will attach themselves to him, and his friends will be many. And they said in the ethical teaching: whoever indulges his own traits, many will pounce upon him. And one may also explain this same matter, "he who separates himself seeks his own desire" — a man separated from every brother and companion, it is desire that he seeks; and because he seeks to go after his own will, therefore his companions have grown distant from him, as in (Proverbs 19:4), "but the poor man is separated from his friend." "He breaks out against all sound wisdom" — one who follows his own desire will not sin in one thing alone, but will break out against everything in the Torah, for he will transgress all of it — in the sense of (Proverbs 20:3), "but every fool will break out."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:32: And there is a further benefit to be found for him in breaking physical desire: for if his desire should ask of him some worthless and sinful thing, he can say to his own heart: Behold, even in what is permitted I do not fulfill my desire — how then shall I stretch out my hand to what is forbidden?
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:33: And there is found in breaking desire a further, mighty benefit: for by it he reveals the sincerity of his heart and the goodness of his intent toward teshuvah, since he despises the very nature that caused him to sin, and by this he finds favor with the Blessed Name and finds grace in His eyes. And so it is written (Psalms 51:19), "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and crushed heart, O God, You will not despise." "A broken spirit" is the lowered and submissive spirit, and "a broken heart" refers to the breaking of physical desire, for desire is placed in the heart, as it is said (Psalms 21:3), "You have given him his heart's desire." And this verse is stated in the psalm of teshuvah; and by its saying, "a broken and crushed heart, O God, You will not despise," we learn that the penitent finds favor with the Lord through the breaking of physical desire, and that this is among the foundations of teshuvah. And further it is said concerning teshuvah (Isaiah 57:15), "to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite."
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:34: And our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever possesses these three traits is of the disciples of Abraham our father — a good eye, a lowly spirit, and a humble soul. The matter of "a humble soul" is that he does not follow after physical desire even in permitted matters, as we find that Abraham said (Genesis 12:11), "Behold now, I know that you are a woman of beautiful appearance" — showing that he had not gazed upon her until that day so as to consider the character of her beauty. And our Sages of blessed memory said regarding what is written (II Samuel 20:3), "and they were confined until the day of their death, widows in living widowhood" — that every day David would command that their hair be dressed and cosmetics given them to adorn them, in order to provoke his own desire and subdue it, so that in overpowering his inclination toward them, atonement might be granted him for the matter of Bathsheba.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:35: The Tenth Foundation – To Better His Deeds in the Very Matter in Which He Acted Presumptuously: if he gazed at forbidden sights, let him conduct himself with lowered eyes; if he sinned through evil speech, let him occupy himself with Torah; and in every limb with which he sinned, let him strive to fulfill the commandments through it. And so our Sages of blessed memory said: the righteous find favor through the very matter in which they had sinned. They further said: if you committed bundles of transgressions, do bundles upon bundles of good deeds to counter them. Feet swift to run to evil — let them run swiftly to a matter of mitzvah. A tongue of falsehood — let his palate utter truth, and let his mouth open in wisdom, and the teaching of kindness be upon his tongue. Hands that shed blood — let him open wide his hand to his brother, to the poor. Haughty eyes — let them be lowered and downcast. A heart that devises wicked thoughts — let him hide the words of Torah in his heart, and let the meditation of his heart be understanding. One who sends forth strife among brothers — let him pursue and seek peace.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:36: The Eleventh Foundation – Searching His Ways: as it is said (Lamentations 3:40), "Let us search and examine our ways, and return to the Lord." And he should do this for three reasons. The first: so that he remember all the things in which he sinned and confess upon all of them, for confession is among the foundations of atonement. The second: so that he know how many are his iniquities and sins, and add to his submission. And the third: because even though he has accepted upon himself to abandon every sin, he must know the specific things in which he sinned, in order to make fences around them and to guard himself very carefully against them from the ambush of the inclination, for his soul is especially prone to stumble in them, since they have become trivial in his eyes and his inclination has gained mastery over him in them; and thus his soul is sick from those deeds, and just as a sick man beginning to recover must guard against many things lest they return him to his illness, so must he.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:37: The Twelfth Foundation – He Must Investigate and Know and Recognize the Severity of the Punishment for Each of His Iniquities: for which of them is there lashing, for which is there liability of excision (karet), and for which is there liability of death by the court — so that he may know the greatness of his iniquity when he confesses, and weep bitterly for having provoked such bitterness, and so that he add further to his submission, and so that he fear his iniquities; for concerning grave transgressions, teshuvah suspends atonement and sufferings scour it away. And so it is written (Jeremiah 2:23), "See your way in the valley, know what you have done." And this foundation will be explained in the Third Gate.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:38: The Thirteenth Foundation – To Regard Light Transgressions as Grave in His Own Eyes: for four reasons. The first: he ought not look to the smallness of the transgression, but rather to the greatness of the One who warned against it. The second: because the inclination has mastery over light transgressions, and this may become a cause for persisting in them, so that they too will come to be reckoned as grave, once the punishment accumulates each time — and they compared this to a thread of silk, which is weak and slight, but when doubled many times over, it becomes a strong cord. The third: because through his persistence in a transgression, it becomes to him as though permitted, and he casts off its yoke and does not guard against it, and he is reckoned among those who cast off the yoke and deny in one matter. And the fourth: for if the inclination defeats him in a small matter, tomorrow it will defeat him in a great matter, as our Sages of blessed memory said: whoever breaks vessels in his anger, regard him in your eyes as though he worshipped idols, for such is the way of the evil inclination — today it tells him to do this, tomorrow it tells him: go worship other gods. And it is said (Genesis 4:6-7), "Is it not so, that if you improve, [there will be] uplift..." Its meaning: why has your countenance fallen? Is it not so, that if you improve your deeds and return to Me, there will be uplift — meaning, your face will be lifted up, as in (Job 11:15), "then you will surely lift up your face without blemish" — or one may interpret this in the sense of forgiveness. "And if you do not improve, sin crouches at the door" — and if you do not turn back from what you have sinned, it is not the iniquity already in your hand alone that will lodge with you, for the inclination crouches at the door to make you sin wherever you go, and it will defeat you continually, since it has already defeated you once and ensnared you, and you have indeed been caught and have not returned; "and to you is its desire" — to lead you astray, and it lies in ambush for you at all times; "but you shall rule over it" — if you wish to overpower it. Therefore you will be punished for the sin, since I have given you the ability to conquer your inclination.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:39: And Solomon the king, peace upon him, said (Proverbs 13:13), "Whoever scorns a matter will be pledged to it, but whoever fears a commandment will be rewarded." He said this of one who scorns light transgressions, for he will be pledged over it for the reasons we have mentioned; "whoever fears a commandment" — who is as afraid to neglect a commandment as he is to fear a grave transgression — "will be rewarded" — he is destined for complete reward. And our Sages of blessed memory said: be as careful with a light commandment as with a grave one. They further said that a commandment draws another commandment in its wake, and a transgression draws another transgression in its wake, for the reward of a commandment is a commandment, and the reward of a transgression is a transgression.
Sha'arei Teshuvah 1:40: The Fourteenth Foundation – Confession: as it is said (Leviticus 5:5), "and he shall confess that in which he has sinned." And he is obligated to mention his own iniquities and the iniquities of his fathers, for he is punished for them when he continues to hold onto the deeds of his fathers; and so it is written (Leviticus 26:40), "And they shall confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers."
